newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate passes scaled-back national parks bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate passes scaled-back national parks bill.

text.p: In one of its last acts of the year the Senate Thursday passed a scaled-down version of a bill to add or expand a number of national parks, readying it for President Clinton's signature.
After a tense afternoon during which the White House and a senator tussled over an agreement to allow the bill to move, the Senate passed the measure on a voice vote.
Clinton said he was pleased with the Senate's action although he called the bill imperfect.

"This legislation will improve the management of our nation's parks and public lands and protect some of our most valued resources ... though not perfect, this bill represents a great victory for the American people," he said in a written statement.

The bill, identical to one the House passed Saturday, included projects in some 40 states. Among major provisions were turning management of San Francisco's Presidio over to a trust, acquiring the Sterling Forest along the New York/New Jersey border, establishing the Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve in Kansas, and establishing a Selma-to-Alabama National Historic Trail in Alabama.
Sen. Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, had held up the bill to try to get concessions for loggers in Southeast Alaska's Tongass National Forest.

After several days of negotiations and hours before the Senate was slated to adjourn, Murkowski got an agreement from the White House that he said would keep a timber supply from the Tongass National Forest flowing to two southeast Alaska sawmills for two years.
While tangles over wording of the deal pushed back the Senate's scheduled adjournment by an hour, Murkowski finally agreed to lift his hold on the parks bill and allow the vote.

The bill had a tortuous history as the White House had threatened to veto the original version, objecting to concessions Murkowski sought for Alaska's loggers as well as a number of land swaps and other measures that it said would hurt the parks system.
But the administration endorsed the scaled-back version, which also was backed by the National Parks Association and a number of environmental groups.
The final bill also dropped a controversial plan to raise revenue for parks by allowing corporations to become licensed parks sponsors, and use that in their advertising.

However the bill kept a measure the White House cited in its veto threat letter which would ease restrictions against development on some Florida barrier islands, and allow those areas to get federal flood insurance.
Several environmental and taxpayer groups opposed that measure, saying it would ruin sensitive beaches and subsidize unwise development in hurricane- and flood-prone areas.
In the deal with Murkowski, the White House agreed to cancel the U.S. Forest Service's contract with Louisiana-Pacific Corp's Ketchikan Pulp Mill, which the company planned to close soon.

Timber from the Tongass National Forest under contract to the pulp mill -- about 300 million board feet or a two-year supply for two Southeast Alaska sawmills -- would be released for competitive bidding.
Murkowski first had pushed to extend the Ketchikan timber contract for another 15 years, then insisted on providing some timber to the sawmills after the pulp mill's contract ended.
Environmental groups opposed the contract extension, saying it perpetuated a sweetheart deal for Ketchikan.
